extracted.intended_audience: general news readers and media professionals interested in journalism ethics and media coverage of campus sexual assault
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing standards and failures in journalistic reporting, editing, supervision, and fact-checking—especially for sensitive stories such as campus sexual-assault allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic failure: avoidable procedural and institutional failures
rubrics_metrics.description: The story was a 'journalistic failure that was avoidable' resulting from failures in reporting, editing, editorial supervision and fact-checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Columbia report emphasized that 'every single person at every level' had opportunities to question things more deeply and pull the strings harder; failures were both individual and procedural/institutional rather than purely unforeseeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting standards: verify core facts and source existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must verify the existence and identity of key sources and core facts before publication (example: the lifeguard named by the subject was not verified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editors allowed the story to run without knowing the lifeguard’s name or 'verifying his existence.' After publication the reporter could not get a correct last name — an internal alarm bell that should have prevented publication. Verification of names, roles, and existence of central actors is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing and editorial supervision: active skepticism and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and supervisors must actively question reporting, not simply accommodate a compelling source narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dana and the report said editors and others had opportunities to 'question things a little more deeply.' Editorial supervision should include pressing for verification and not deferring to reporter/source assertions when important details are unconfirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking: rigorous pre-publication fact checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-checking must catch inconsistencies and unverified claims prior to publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report faulted failures in fact-checking that allowed key inconsistencies to remain; internal doubts that arose after publication indicate fact-checking did not adequately resolve open questions beforehand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing empathy with verification: 'believe the victim' should not suspend verification
rubrics_metrics.description: While respecting victims and avoiding retraumatization is important, a desire to 'believe the victim' should not override the journalist’s responsibility to verify and corroborate claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report noted editors and the reporter were 'too accommodating' of the subject because she described herself as a survivor. It cites social-science advice to respect autonomy and avoid retraumatization, but stresses survivors 'are as reliable in their testimony as other crime victims' and verification remains necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trauma-informed reporting: respect autonomy and avoid retraumatizing sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should be mindful of trauma-informed practices—respecting victims’ autonomy and avoiding retraumatization—while still pursuing verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report references social scientists and trauma specialists who urge respect for survivor autonomy and caution against retraumatizing interviewing techniques; this must be balanced with the obligation to get facts right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections, apologies, and retractions: accountability after errors
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting failures are identified, publications should apologize to readers and affected parties and issue corrections or retractions as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rolling Stone retracted the piece and the managing editor issued an apology to readers and those damaged by the story; the reporter also issued a public apology acknowledging responsibility and the need to 'get it right.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional response: evaluate need for systemic change vs incremental fixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether failures reflect isolated individual mistakes or systemic problems that require changes to editorial systems and processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report framed the failure as both individual and procedural; however, top editors expressed the belief that an overhaul of systems was unnecessary and that doing the same processes 'and just make sure we don’t make this mistake again' would suffice — highlighting tension about appropriate organizational remediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal red flags after publication indicate pre-publication process breakdowns
rubrics_metrics.description: Doubts or alarms that arise internally after publication (e.g., reporter expressing surprise that a subject could not name a key alleged perpetrator) are indicators that the pre-publication process failed to surface and resolve significant inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recounts the reporter saying 'An alarm bell went off in my head' when the subject could not spell the alleged perpetrator’s last name; such post-publication doubts should have been raised and resolved prior to publishing.
